text: Chapter 2 built Northbridge Retail's first pipelines in GitHub Actions. This chapter rebuilds the same ideas in Azure DevOps — the other major platform you'll meet on the job, and the one many larger enterprises already run their work tracking and source control on. This lesson is the map before we start building anything.

Azure DevOps isn't Azure the cloud platform, even though the name suggests it — it's a separate delivery platform with five services. Boards tracks work items, backlogs, and sprints. Repos holds Git source control and pull requests. Pipelines handles build and release automation, which is this whole chapter's focus. Test Plans covers manual testing, outside this course. And Artifacts shares package output across pipelines. A team doesn't have to use all five together — plenty run Azure Pipelines against a GitHub repo instead of Azure Repos.

Here's that navigation inside a real Azure DevOps project — Boards, Repos, Pipelines, and the rest, all one click apart in the left-hand sidebar. Every project you ever open in Azure DevOps starts from this same layout.

Everything lives under an organization, usually one per company, which contains one or more projects. Northbridge Retail's engineers work inside a project called storefront, holding their Boards backlog, their storefront-api Git repository, and every pipeline this chapter builds, all in one place.

Azure Pipelines offers two formats for defining a pipeline. YAML pipelines are defined in a file checked into the repo, version-controlled and reviewable in a pull request. The older Classic designer builds pipelines visually in the browser, with nothing checked into source control. This course uses YAML exclusively — a pipeline that isn't version-controlled can't be code-reviewed, diffed, or rolled back like the application code it ships.
Next lesson, we write storefront-api's first azure-pipelines.yml from scratch, piece by piece.
